assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Degrees of freedom
items.clue: Number of categories minus 1 in a χ² calculation.

items.label: Operculum
items.clue: Bony flap covering the gills on each side of a fish's head

items.label: Internal intercostal muscles
items.clue: Contract only in forced breathing out, pulling the ribs down and in

items.label: Hinge cells
items.clue: In marram grass these lose water in dry wind, so the leaf rolls up.

questions.stem: Mammalian lungs contain a branched network of bronchioles ending in millions of alveoli. How does this branching contribute to gas exchange?

options.text: It multiplies the area of airway wall across which gases are exchanged into the blood as air travels inward.
It packs a very large alveolar surface, each part close to a capillary bed, into the volume of the thorax.
It lets the lungs grow larger, and a larger organ must have a bigger surface for gas exchange.
It houses the muscle that contracts to pump air in and out of the alveoli found at the end of every branch.

questions.stem: In a model of one gill lamella, water enters with a relative O₂ concentration of 100 and blood enters with 0. Water and blood flow at equal rates and carry O₂ equally well. What is the highest value the blood could reach with each type of flow?

options.text: 100 with parallel flow; 100 with counter-current flow
50 with parallel flow; 50 with counter-current flow
50 with parallel flow; close to 100 with counter-current flow
Close to 100 with parallel flow; 50 with counter-current flow

questions.explanation: Parallel flow stops at equilibrium, 50. Counter-current flow keeps a gradient all along, so blood approaches the 100 of incoming water.

questions.stem: A student measures the lengths of 20 leaves from plants growing in the sun and 20 from plants growing in the shade. She wants to know whether mean leaf length differs between the two. Which statistical test should she use?

options.text: Chi-squared, because she is comparing two groups of plants.
Student's t-test, because she is comparing the means of two sets of continuous data.
A correlation coefficient, because she wants to know whether light is related to leaf length.
No test is needed: if the two means differ, the difference is real.

questions.explanation: Two groups, one measured variable, a difference in means: that is what the t-test is for.

questions.stem: Which sequence of events draws air into the lungs during inspiration?

options.text: Air entering the lungs inflates them, and the inflating lungs push the ribs outward and the diaphragm downward.
The muscular walls of the lungs contract, widening the alveoli and sucking air in through the trachea.
The diaphragm and external intercostals contract, thorax volume rises and lung pressure falls.
The diaphragm relaxes and rises into a dome, and the ribs move up so that air is drawn in to fill the space.

questions.explanation: Larger thorax volume, pressure in the lungs below atmospheric, and air flows in down the pressure gradient.

questions.stem: A 1999 study found that children who had slept with a light on before the age of two were more likely to become short-sighted later. Later studies found that short-sighted parents were more likely to leave a light on at night, and short sight is partly inherited. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Night-time lighting causes short sight, because the 1999 correlation was found in a large group of children.
The correlation can be explained by parents' short sight, which is linked to both variables.
The 1999 correlation must have been a mistake: the children with night lights were not really more short-sighted.
The later studies prove that light at night has no effect on the eye at all.
